Spec: Fast Corrective + Self-RAG Document
Q&A (LangGraph)
​Oct 24, 2026 · ​@Rup
Overview and goals
The system answers a user's question across one or more uploaded documents (typed
PDFs, scanned PDFs, or handwritten pages read via OCR) using a LangGraph workflow
that combines Corrective RAG (CRAG) with a Self-RAG / LLM-as-a-Judge check. It ships
as a self-contained, versioned REST API so the separate backend team can call it without
touching its internals, and it must stay fast: a typical answer lands in under about 6
seconds.
Goals
Answer questions grounded in one or many uploaded documents (typed, scanned or
handwritten), with document- and page-level citations.
Detect weak retrieval and correct it: rewrite the query, and fall back to web search
when the document chunks grade too poorly.

when the document chunks grade too poorly.
Verify the final answer for grounding (no hallucination) and usefulness (actually
answers the question) before returning it.
Keep latency low by grading all retrieved chunks in one batched LLM call instead of
one call per chunk.
Non-goals (v1)
User accounts, billing or the main product UI (owned by the backend team).
Multi-turn chat memory (each query is answered independently).
Non-English handwriting (v2).
Latency targets

Integration contract for the backend team
OpenAPI: FastAPI publishes /openapi.json and /docs ; the backend can generate a
typed client from it.
Versioning: all routes under /v1 ; breaking changes go to /v2 , never into /v1 .
Auth: service-to-service API key in the X-API-Key header; the backend handles end-
user auth and passes an optional X-User-Id for logging only.
Stateless API: no state in process memory; files, indexes and job status live behind
store interfaces (local disk + FAISS for dev, S3 + Qdrant/pgvector + Redis for prod)
chosen by config.
Async ingestion: uploads return 202 + job_id immediately; OCR and indexing run in a
worker (Celery/RQ or FastAPI background tasks for v1). Optional callback_url gets a

worker (Celery/RQ or FastAPI background tasks for v1). Optional callback_url gets a
POST when the job finishes.
Errors: one JSON shape for every failure: {"error": {"code": "DOC_NOT_READY",
"message": "...", "request_id": "..."}} , with codes such as DOC_NOT_READY ,
UNSUPPORTED_FILE , OCR_FAILED , TIMEOUT .
Config by environment: model names, API keys, store URLs and limits come from env
vars overriding config.yaml ; no code change to deploy elsewhere.
Observability: every response carries request_id ; per-node timings go to LangSmith
and structured logs.
Because core/service.py has no web dependencies, the same functions can also be
imported directly as a library if the backend team prefers in-process calls over HTTP.
Spec: Fast Corrective + Self-RAG PDF Q&A (LangGraph)
Page 4 of 14

Architecture
The system has two parts: a one-time ingestion pipeline per uploaded file, and the
LangGraph query graph below that runs per question.
Ingestion (once per uploaded file, in the background worker): each page is routed by
type, so typed pages stay fast and only scanned or handwritten pages pay the OCR cost.
1. Detect: for each page, check the PDF text layer with PyMuPDF. More than about 50
characters of real text → text page; otherwise (or an image upload) → OCR page.
2. Pre-process OCR pages: render at 300 DPI, deskew, denoise, boost contrast
(OpenCV).
3. Classify printed vs handwritten: a cheap first pass with the printed-text OCR engine;
low mean confidence (below 0.6) marks the page handwritten .

low mean confidence (below 0.6) marks the page handwritten .
4. OCR: printed scans → PaddleOCR (local, fast). Handwritten pages → a vision LLM (e.g.
GPT-4o-mini / Gemini Flash) prompted to transcribe exactly, or Azure Document
Intelligence Read; chosen via the OcrProvider config. Pages run in parallel, up to 8 at a
time.
5. Chunk + index: chunk the text (keeping doc_id , filename, page, ocr ,
ocr_confidence in metadata), embed into the collection's vector index, update the
BM25 index, cache by file hash.
Pages with OCR confidence below 0.4 are still indexed but flagged, and the generator is
told to treat them cautiously.

{"grounded": true, "answers_question": true, "reason": "All claims trace to 
chunks c_3 and c_7."}
Combining the hallucination check and the answer-relevance check in one call saves a full
LLM round-trip compared with classic Self-RAG, which runs them as two graders.
Batch grading design
All retrieved chunks go to the grader in a single LLM call that returns a score per chunk,
turning 8 sequential calls (about 8 × 0.6 s) into one call of roughly 0.8–1.2 s.
How it works
1. Number each chunk with a short ID ( c_0 … c_7 ) and trim each to at most 400 tokens.
2. Send the question plus all numbered chunks in one prompt.
3. Force structured output (Pydantic schema / JSON mode) so the response parses
without retries.

3. Force structured output (Pydantic schema / JSON mode) so the response parses
without retries.
4. Score each chunk 0–2 rather than yes/no, so CRAG can tell "correct" from "ambiguous".
Output schema
class ChunkGrade(BaseModel):
    chunk_id: str
    score: Literal[0, 1, 2]   # 0 = irrelevant, 1 = partial, 2 = directly 
answers
class BatchGrades(BaseModel):
    grades: list[ChunkGrade]
Prompt (system)
You grade document chunks for relevance to a question.
For EACH chunk id, return a score:
2 = contains information that directly helps answer the question
1 = related but only partially useful
0 = not relevant
Judge each chunk independently. Return every chunk id exactly once.
Guardrails
Batch size: up to 10 chunks per call. If retrieval returns more, split into parallel batches

Guardrails
Batch size: up to 10 chunks per call. If retrieval returns more, split into parallel batches
with asyncio.gather , not sequential calls.
Missing or duplicate IDs in the response: treat missing as score 0; never re-call the
grader.

Page 10 of 14

Latency budget and speed optimizations
The happy path spends about 3.5 s across four steps; every optimization below targets
either the number of LLM calls or the time the user waits before seeing text.
Optimizations, in order of impact
1. Batch grading: one grader call for all chunks instead of one per chunk (the core
requirement).
2. Small model for control steps: grader, rewriter and judge use a fast model; only
generate uses the larger one.
3. Merged judge: grounding and answer-relevance checked in one structured call.
4. Speculative web search (optional flag): run web_search on the original query in
parallel with batch_grade via LangGraph fan-out, and discard the results if grading
says "correct". Trades one cheap search call for about 1 s saved on the fallback path.

says "correct". Trades one cheap search call for about 1 s saved on the fallback path.
5. Stream the answer: stream generate tokens to the client; show a "verifying" badge
until the judge returns, and replace the answer only if the judge fails.
6. Ingestion done once: chunking and embeddings are computed at upload and cached
by PDF hash; re-uploads skip ingestion.
7. Answer cache: cache (doc_id, normalized question) → answer object for repeated
questions.
8. Tight context: pass only chunks scoring 1–2 to generate , trimmed, which shortens
prompts and generation time.
Tech stack, config and delivery
The stack is Python with LangGraph for orchestration and FastAPI for serving; every
threshold above lives in one config file.

Error handling
LLM call fails or times out (5 s per call): retry once, then skip that step (e.g. no judge →
return answer with verdict unknown).
Web search fails: answer from document chunks with a caveat that the documents
may not cover the question.

Web search fails: answer from document chunks with a caveat that the documents
may not cover the question.
Malformed grader JSON: treat all chunks as score 1 (ambiguous path).
OCR fails on a page: mark the page failed, index the rest, report it in the job status; the
document still becomes ready .
Query on a collection with no ready documents: return DOC_NOT_READY (HTTP 409)
instead of waiting.
Evaluation
Test set: 60 question–answer pairs over 5 sample files (3 typed PDFs, 1 scanned PDF, 1
set of handwritten notes), including 10 questions the documents cannot answer
(should route to web) and 10 that need two documents together.
Track: answer correctness, faithfulness (RAGAS), route accuracy, p50 / p95 latency,
LLM calls per query.
